newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar immobile in Tokyo due to overseas holidays.
newsitem.headline: Dollar immobile in Tokyo due to overseas holidays.

text.p: The dollar was locked in a tight range against the yen and the mark in Tokyo on Friday due to closure of many centres for the long Easter holiday.

Dollar-buying spree ebbed due to caution ahead of a variety of events next week, including U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's visit to Japan and Bank of Japan's quarterly business survey, although longer-term view stays bullish for the dollar.

"Many operators were loath to take up fresh positions here and carry them over due to risks that they cannot cover their positions later today due to the closure of overseas markets," said a senior trader at a European bank in Tokyo.
Activity here was limited to cross-driven trade, with solid mark buying for yen by Japanese investors supporting the dollar/yen rate indirectly, dealers said.

Overnight plunge in U.S. stocks and a slew of events next week that are likely to serve as dollar-selling factors also capped the dollar's rise, although were no specific reasons for selling dollars actively from the current level, they said.
"A slew of events next week will in general favour yen buying," said a Japanese bank dealer.

Dealers are worried that tensions over U.S.-Japan bilateral trade may flare up again when U.S. Treasury Robert Rubin visits Japan on April 4. He will stop off in Japan before going on to the APEC forum meeting in the Philippines.

Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers' comments on Thursday that the United States remains worried about a rise in Japan's trade surplus dragged the dollar down against the yen. The Bank of Japan (BOJ) will release its closely watched survey of corporate sentiment or "tankan" on April 2.

"If the BOJ's survey show better-than-expected results for corporate activities and that sparks a rise in Japanese market interest rates, the dollar will fall against the yen in tandem," said a U.S. bank dealer.
He said the expected announcement on Monday of government steps to help boost liquidity in the real estate market will also be closely watched.

However, he and other dealers said the dollar's bottom could be well-supported at the lower end of 122 yen, because of buying interest from Japanese investors related to their offshore investments in the new fiscal year in April.
"There are lots of investors who have failed to buy enough dollars and are waiting for dips," said a Tokyo bank dealer.

Some Japanese investors recently bought dollar three-month call options with strikes of around 130 yen on a perception that the dollar would eventually break through the sensitive level of 125 yen, he added.
But many dealers expect the dollar to stay in a 122-125 yen range for the time being.
